opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we think about a lot, because there's a bit of irony in it. We spend all day building silicon to make AI inference faster and more efficient for everyone else, so we'd better be practicing what we preach internally.

The way I think about it is in a few layers. The first layer is just everyday productivity. Every knowledge worker at d-Matrix, whether they're in engineering, sales, finance, or HR, should be using these tools to write, summarize, research, and get through the routine work faster. That's table stakes now. We encourage people to experiment, and we try not to be overly prescriptive, because people discover the most useful workflows on their own.

The second layer, which is more interesting for a company like ours, is engineering. Chip design is incredibly complex. You have RTL design, verification, physical design, software stacks, compilers, kernels. A huge amount of time goes into verification and debugging. That's where AI-assisted coding and AI-assisted verification can make a real difference. Our software team uses coding assistants heavily, and we're looking closely at how AI can help hardware engineers generate test cases, triage failures, and get through regression results faster. When a tape-out costs what it does, anything that shortens the cycle or catches a bug earlier pays for itself many times over.

The third layer is cultural. You can't just hand people tools and declare victory. You have to give them permission to change how they work, and leaders have to model it. I use these tools myself every day. When the CEO is doing that visibly, it sends a signal that this isn't a side experiment, it's how we operate.

And then there's guardrails. We're a semiconductor company, and our IP is everything. So we're careful about what data goes where, which models we use for which tasks, and we lean toward setups where sensitive design data stays within our control. That's actually one of the reasons I'm so bullish on efficient inference in general. As inference gets cheaper and faster, enterprises will be able to run capable models closer to their own data, and that changes the adoption equation for companies like ours and for our customers.

So in short, broad adoption for productivity, deep adoption where it accelerates engineering, and a culture that treats AI as a core part of how we build, all with the right guardrails around our IP.

r001.rationale: The response says employees “should be using” AI tools and calls it “table stakes,” but also says d-Matrix encourages experimentation and avoids being overly prescriptive. It does not clearly state that adoption is mandatory.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that we think about it in two layers, because d-Matrix sits in a slightly unusual position: we build inference hardware for AI, so AI isn't just a tool we adopt, it's the thing we're building for. Those two layers inform each other constantly.

The first layer is internal adoption, the way any company would think about it. Chip design is an incredibly long, expensive, iterative process. You tape out a chip and you don't get a second chance for a very long time, so anything that compresses the loop between an idea and a verified design is enormously valuable. We've leaned into AI for things like verification, where you're writing enormous amounts of test code and chasing corner cases, and for the software stack, where our compiler and runtime teams use coding assistants every day. We're a relatively small company competing against very large incumbents, so leverage per engineer is everything. If AI lets a team of ten do what used to take thirty, that's existential for us, not a nice-to-have.

The second layer is that we are our own customer. Every model we run internally, every agentic workflow, every assistant an engineer uses, is a data point about what inference actually looks like in practice. Batch sizes, context lengths, latency sensitivity, how often a token is really needed in a hundred milliseconds versus a second. A lot of the industry built on assumptions from training, where throughput is king. Inference is a different animal. It's memory-bound, it's latency-sensitive, and it's economically unforgiving because you pay for it every single time someone asks a question. Using these tools ourselves keeps us honest about what the workload is, rather than what a benchmark says it is.

I'll also say we try to be disciplined about where we don't adopt it. The failure mode I see in a lot of companies is treating AI as a mandate from the top, where everyone has to use it somewhere. We'd rather start from the bottleneck. Where is the engineer waiting? Where is the loop slow? If AI helps there, great. If it doesn't, we move on. The teams that have gotten the most out of it are the ones who found a specific pain and attacked it, not the ones who were told to go find a use case.

And culturally, we've tried to make it safe to experiment and safe to say something didn't work. The tools are changing every few months. What was a toy last year is genuinely useful now, and some of what's hyped today won't pan out. You want an organization that keeps re-evaluating rather than deciding once and locking in.

r001.rationale: The candidate says d-Matrix avoids treating AI as a company-wide mandate and instead adopts it where it addresses a specific bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in two ways. One is the technology we’re building, and the other is how we use AI ourselves to work more effectively. We have to apply that same curiosity internally: Where can AI help an engineer move faster? Where can it help a team find information or take repetitive work off someone’s plate?

The approach I favor is to start with specific problems, give people room to experiment, and measure whether it actually helps. You also need people to check the output, especially when the cost of a mistake is high. The goal is to make AI a useful part of how we work, with human judgment still central to the process.

r001.rationale: The response says d-Matrix should explore internal AI use and make AI a useful part of work, but does not state that AI adoption across the company is mandatory.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it in two ways. One is the product we’re building—helping our customers run AI inference efficiently. The other is how we use AI ourselves to make our teams more productive.

Internally, I think the right approach is to start with specific problems. Where can AI help an engineer write or review code? Where can it help someone find information or get through a repetitive task? Give people room to experiment, but measure whether it actually improves the work. You still need human judgment and accountability, particularly when you’re designing hardware.

The goal is to make AI part of how we work, with the same discipline we bring to any other tool: understand where it helps, understand its limitations, and build on what works.

r001.rationale: The response describes experimenting with AI and measuring its benefits, but does not state that adoption across d-Matrix is mandatory.
